attributes.title: Level 2

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set vy to 0  in the Player sprite’s [move sprite with buttons] block?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ Did you drag the [move sprite with buttons] block inside the [on start] container block?

❓ Did you drag the [set sprite stay in screen]  block inside the [on start] container block?

❓ If you wanted the Player sprite to only move up and down, what would you change?


Sensei Pro Tip: 

💡 Remind ninjas to select the correct sprite name in the new blocks.
steps.instructions:
Begin the Space Adventure!


There are already code blocks in the [on start] container block.


Code the Player sprite to move with the direction buttons on the MakeCode game controller, and keep it from moving off the screen!


Set the Player sprite to only move left and right by clicking the + on the [move sprite with buttons] block. Delete the ‘100’ in the vy parameter bubble and type 0.


Click ▶ then use the on-screen direction buttons to move the Player sprite left and right across the screen.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you move the Enemy sprite’s blocks to the [on game update every ms] loop and change the sprite name in [set sprite velocity to] block?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ What do you notice about the speed and direction of how the Enemy sprites move across the screen? 

❓Why might it be helpful to move the Enemy sprite’s blocks into an [on game update every ms] loop?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The [on game update every ms] adds a loop into the code. This means that the actions within the container block will repeat continuously, every 500 ms (0.5 seconds) while the game is played.
steps.instructions:
Use a loop to make lots of Enemy sprites appear!


Open the Game code block menu, then drag out an [on game update every ms] loop. Drag the Enemy sprite’s [set sprite to] and [set position to] blocks out of the [on start] container block into the [on game update every ms] loop. 


Open the Sprites code block menu and drag out a [set sprite velocity to] block into the [on game update every ms] loop, then select the Enemy sprite’s name.


Click ▶ to see the Enemy sprite repeatedly appear and move diagonally to the bottom right corner!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you change the value in the [on game update every ms] loop to a number bigger than 500 ms?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ Did you tinker with the time length parameter in the the [on game update]loop? 

❓What did you observe about the number of Enemy sprites on the screen as you tried out different lengths of time?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Help the ninja notice that the time parameter in the [on game update every ms] loop is presented in milliseconds (ms). This means that if they’d like something to repeat continuously every 1 second, it will show up as 1000 ms.
steps.instructions:
Too many Enemy sprites are on the screen!


Change the parameter in the [on game update every ms] loop, by selecting a different value from the drop down, to change how often the code inside the loop runs.


Click ▶ to see how changing the parameter changes the number of Enemy sprites on the screen.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you drag a [pick random] value block in the x parameter bubble of the Enemy’s [set position to] block and change the values?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ Why might you want the Enemy sprites to begin at different positions in your game?

❓Why would you want to edit the x value parameter and not the y value parameter?

❓What other blocks could you add randomness to?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Randomness can introduce a fun element of surprise into a ninja’s project. Guide the ninja to tinker with x values within the [pick random] value block to explore its effects.

💡Guide the ninja to notice that the two parameters indicate a range of possible numbers from a lower valued number to a greater valued number.
steps.instructions:
Code each new Enemy sprite to start in a random position!


Open the Math code block menu, then drag out a [pick random] value block and insert it into the x value parameter for the [set sprite position to] block.


Change the numbers to 0 and 160 so the Enemy sprites will start somewhere between the far left and far right sides of the screen.


Click ▶ to see Enemy sprites start in different positions as they come down from the top.

steps.hints: ❓ What sprite did you select to bounce on the wall?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ How does the [set sprite bounce on wall] block change the Enemy sprite’s movement? Why does it make the game more fun to play?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Help the ninja notice the connection between the [set sprite bounce on wall] and the [set sprite stay in screen] blocks. Prompt the ninja to identify the similarities and reflect on why you might use one block instead of the other.
steps.instructions:
Make the game more exciting by setting the Enemy sprites to bounce on the screen walls!


Open the Sprites code block menu, then drag out a [set sprite bounce on wall] block into the [on game update every ms] loop. 


Click ▶ to see the screen fill with Enemy sprites!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you change the sprite kind parameters so the [on sprite overlaps sprite] checks if the Player overlaps the Enemy, and then destroys the otherSprite?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


﻿Ask the ninja:

❓ Did you click the + to select a special effect when the sprite is destroyed?

❓ Did you drag the otherSprite bubble from the [on sprite overlaps sprite] block into the [destroy sprite] block?

❓ Did you test out different effects and sounds and select ones that you like?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The sprite kind information will be used instead of the sprite names in the [on sprite overlaps sprite] container block. Instead of specifying one sprite, the overlap code will affect all sprites of a certain kind.

💡 Remind the ninja that the time parameter is presented in milliseconds (ms) and that 1000 ms is equal to 1 second.
steps.instructions:
Code the Enemy sprite to self-destruct and make a sound when it overlaps with the Player sprite!


Open the Sprites code block menu then drag out an [on sprite overlaps sprite] container block. 


Change the (otherSprite) kind to Enemy, then destroy the (otherSprite) and play a sound when the Player and Enemy sprites overlap. Click + on the [destroy sprite] block to change the effect parameter.


Click ▶ to see what happens when the Enemy sprites touch the Player sprite.

steps.hints:
❓ Did you select the Player sprite’s name in the [set projectile to projectile from sprite] block?


You can also use Z or the space bar on your keyboard to launch the projectile:
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓Did you select or draw your own Projectile image? What might you want to include in the design?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Since the projectile is flying up, it makes sense for the image of the projectile to look like a line or skinny rectangle/oval shape.
steps.instructions:
Give the Player a chance to fend off the Enemy! 


Open the Controller code block menu and drag out an [on A button pressed] container block.  


Open the Sprites code block menu and drag a [set projectile to projectile from sprite] block into the [on A button pressed] container block. A projectile is an object in motion.


Click the gray square and select or draw an image for the Projectile sprite. In the second dropdown, select the Player sprite’s name.


Click ▶ then use the A button to see the Projectile being launched from the Player sprite!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you change the projectile’s vx and vy values?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ What do you notice about the Projectile’s direction when you change the vy value from a number greater than zero, to one that is less than zero?

❓ What would you change to make the Projectile move down, instead of up? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Guide ninjas to notice that the y value increases as the projectile moves down so a negative value moves a projectile sprite up. A ninja may choose to test out different negative values in the vy parameter.
steps.instructions:
Ready, aim, fire!


Change the vx and vy parameters so the Projectile moves up vertically instead of diagonally. Update vx to 0 and vy to -50. 


Click ▶ then use the A button to see the Projectile sprite being launched up!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you change the sprite kind parameters so the [on sprite overlaps sprite] checks if the Projectile overlaps the Enemy, and then destroys the otherSprite?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:❓ Did you click the + to select a special effect when the sprite is destroyed?❓ Did you drag the otherSprite bubble from the [on sprite overlaps sprite] block into the [destroy sprite] block?

Sensei Pro Tip:💡 Guide ninjas to recognize why using the sprite kind information is helpful in this situation. Instead of just destroying one Enemy sprite, the Projectile will destroy any Enemy sprite kind when it overlaps with it.
steps.instructions:
Code the Enemy sprite to self-destruct and make a sound when it overlaps with the Projectile sprite!


Drag in a second [on sprite overlaps sprite] container block, select “Projectile'' as the first sprite kind and “Enemy” as the other (second) sprite kind.


Then, destroy the (otherSprite) and play a sound when the Projectile and Enemy sprites overlap. Click + on the [destroy sprite] block to change the effect parameter.


Click ▶ then use the A button to see the Enemy sprite disappear when the Projectile overlaps with it!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you check where you set variables versus where you change variables?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:❓ Did you add the [change life by] and [change score by] blocks into the correct [on sprite overlaps sprite] containers?❓ What else could happen when the Player sprite earns a point or loses a life? How does the Player sprite win the game?

Sensei Pro Tip:💡Guide the ninja to try out different parameters for the number of lives and how the score changes. Just like with speed and other parameters, there is no perfect number of lives.
steps.instructions:
Add variables to track lives and score!


Drag [set life to] and [set score to] blocks into the [on start] container block.


In the Player overlaps Enemy [on sprite overlaps sprite] container block, drag in a [change life by] block.


In the Projectile overlaps Enemy [on sprite overlaps sprite] container block, drag in a [change score by] block.


Click ▶ then test the game to see the lives and score variables change as the sprites overlap!

steps.hints: ❓Did you add customizations to your game including a background color, screen effect, directions and more?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ Which block will set a background color? Which block will set screen effects? Which block will set dialog boxes?

❓ What directions will help people understand how your project works?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Guide ninjas to note that while these customizing blocks are open ended and not required for the game to “work”, they really improve the Player’s experience playing a game, either by giving context to what the Player should do or not do, or to provide a more fun experience overall. They also allow the Ninja to add their personal touch and express themselves through small details present in the game.
steps.instructions:
Customize this game by setting a background color, adding a screen effect, and adding directions with dialog boxes!


Click ▶ to see the completed game project!

subgroups.introduction: Create a game where the points variable increases as the Player sprite destroys as many Enemy sprites as possible using projectiles!

validationItems.text: Move the Player left and right with the direction buttons, and set the Player sprite to stay in screen.
Use a Game Update loop to create Enemy sprites
Start the Enemy sprite in a random position
Set the Enemy sprite to bounce when it hits a wall
Destroy the Enemy sprite when it overlaps the Player sprite
Player sprite fires a projectile when A button is pressed
Destroy the Enemy sprite when it overlaps a Projectile sprite
Add a life variable, and change it when the Player overlaps an Enemy
Add a score variable, and change it when the Projectile overlaps an Enemy
Add a background color, screen effect, or dialog boxes with game directions

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 2 of Yellow Belt! In this level, you’ll learn about loops, which are chunks of code that repeat a sequence of instructions. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 2:

badges.title: Around and Around
badges.description: Use loops to repeat code in a project.

badges.title: The Times, They Are A-Changin’
badges.description: Use a game update loop to repeat actions in a project.

badges.title: Bouncing off the Walls
badges.description: Set a sprite to bounce on walls in a project.

badges.title: Pew Pew
badges.description: Launch a projectile from a specific sprite.

badges.title: Button Masher
badges.description: Use an event triggered by the A button in a project.

badges.title: I Like to Move It Move It
badges.description: Use velocity to make a sprite move on its own.
